fact_sheet.business_description: The New York Times Company creates a journalism-based product bundle including games, cooking, product recommendations, and sports coverage. It has transitioned from a print-advertising model to a direct digital subscriber relationship, though it maintains legacy print operations. [D01]
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Digital-only subscriptions (11.30 million subscribers) and legacy print subscriptions. [D01, D02]
Bundle/multiproduct offerings (6.02 million users) encourage habitual use and pricing opportunities. [D01]
economics: Second-quarter operating margin of 15.5%, adjusted operating margin 19.5%. [D02]
Operating costs include journalism, product development, and customer acquisition. [D01]
earnings_record: Annual revenue: $2.31 billion (2022), $2.43 billion (2023), $2.59 billion (2024). [D01, D02]
Q2 revenue $685.9 million (+9.7% y/y), operating profit $106.6 million (+34.2%), adjusted operating profit $133.8 million. [D01, D02]
competitive_position: Direct digital subscriber relationship serves as a potential defensible franchise. [D01]
Competes with free news and entertainment bundles. [D06]
Journalism must be renewed continually, and subscriber acquisition costs are rising. [D05, D06]
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Cash and marketable securities of $951.5 million. [D02]
No outstanding debt; $400 million revolving commitment available. [D02]
management_and_capital_allocation: Dual-class governance structure limits outside shareholder influence. [D01, D05]
Capital allocation includes marketing, journalism reinvestment, and managing print-to-digital transition. [D01, D05]
price_and_valuation: Mechanical P/E based on Q2 annualization: 28.70x (GAAP) or 24.74x (adjusted). [D04]

yields_pct.basis: No specific yield figures are stated in the pack; the analyst is instructed to use provided figures only. [D01, D02, D04]

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Rising subscriber acquisition costs (marketing expenses up 12.8% and media promotion up 15.9%). [D05]
Generative AI creating distribution threats and legal conflicts. [D05]
Churn risk as subscribers exit promotional periods. [D05]
Continued decline of print subscriptions. [D03, D05]
recent_events: August 6, 2025: Q2 results reported showing 230,000 net digital additions. [D03]
berkshire_context: Berkshire holds no the Company position as of the latest 13F. [D08]
Berkshire had $344.1 billion in cash/Treasury liquidity as of August 2, 2025. [D08]
missing_data: Maintenance vs. growth capital expenditure split

understandable.evidence: While the transition to a digital subscriber model is clear, the long-term impact of generative AI and competition from free bundles on a journalism-based product creates significant uncertainty about the business model in 10-20 years [D01, D05, D06].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: The direct digital subscriber relationship is a potential franchise, but rising subscriber acquisition costs and competition from free alternatives suggest a moat that requires constant, increasing reinvestment [D01, D05, D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Revenue has grown steadily from $2.31 billion in 2022 to $2.59 billion in 2024, demonstrating consistent performance during the transition from print to digital [D01, D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The company maintains a strong balance sheet with no outstanding debt and $951.5 million in cash and marketable securities [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business requires ongoing, escalating investment in journalism, product development, and customer acquisition to maintain its subscriber base, suggesting high capital intensity for growth [D01, D05].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: The dual-class governance structure limits outside shareholder influence, which complicates an assessment of whether management is fully aligned with all owners [D01, D05].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: At a market capitalization significantly lower than the $5 billion threshold, this would be considered a deputy position for Berkshire [D04].

price_screen.evidence: With a trailing P/E of approximately 25-29x, the implied earnings yield is well below the required threshold for a business facing significant competitive and technological headwinds [D04].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a media enterprise undergoing a difficult digital transition with high reinvestment needs and structural competitive threats.

gate2.why_available: The market correctly identifies this as a business undergoing a difficult digital transition with high, non-discretionary reinvestment needs. There is no evidence of a temporary cloud that masks a durable, low-maintenance franchise; rather, the economics suggest a permanent requirement for heavy spending on journalism and marketing to fend off free digital competition [D01, D05, D06].
evidence: Journalism must be renewed continually with rising subscriber acquisition costs [D05, D06].
P/E ratio of ~25-29x is too expensive for a business requiring constant, escalating reinvestment [D04].
Digital-only ARPU growth of 3.2% is modest relative to the competitive threats and marketing spend [D01, D02, D05].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: That the digital bundle provides a sufficient, low-maintenance moat to justify a ~25-29x earnings multiple despite rising churn risk and AI-driven distribution threats [D04, D05, D06].
what_must_be_true: The business must demonstrate that marketing and journalism reinvestment will eventually stabilize as a lower percentage of revenue.
The digital subscriber base must prove resilient to AI-generated free alternatives.
The valuation must reach a level that provides a margin of safety against the ongoing decline of legacy print operations.

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: not in pack; adjusted operating profit per share approx $0.83 based on Q2 2025 results [D02, D04]

key_assumptions: requires assumption on maintenance capital expenditure [D02]
requires assumption on long-term growth vs print decline [D05]

gate3.price_vs_value: price is 24-28x earnings, significantly above the 10x target for ordinary businesses [D04]
gate3.alternatives: Berkshire has $344.1 billion in cash/Treasuries yielding a risk-free return; this is superior to an expensive, capital-intensive media business [D08]
gate3.downside_case: Permanent loss of competitive advantage due to rising subscriber acquisition costs and AI-driven distribution threats [D05, D06]
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capital expenditure assumed to be a significant portion of total capex due to journalistic requirements
Long-term normalized earnings power is not clearly defined in the pack

gate4.role_description: Berkshire's edge is patience and permanent capital, allowing value to be realized through business compounding and rational capital allocation [D08].
value_realisation_path: Compounding of digital subscriber revenue and efficient management of the print-to-digital transition [D01, D05].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: For marketable securities, Berkshire operates as a permanent passive holder; this is a deputy-sized position given it does not meet the scale requirements to move the needle for Berkshire [D04].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to AI-driven, free information alternatives [D06]
Subscriber acquisition costs increasing faster than ARPU growth, indicating an eroding moat [D05]
Management allocates capital toward non-journalistic growth initiatives outside the core competency [D01]
Structural decline in digital engagement leads to higher churn rates than currently modeled [D05]
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Cash position remains robust at $344.1B [D08]; this position is too small to move the needle and does not meet Berkshire's stringent requirements for durable competitive advantage and valuation [D04].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Capital is better deployed in risk-free Treasuries or retained as cash given the lack of a sufficient margin of safety in this business [D08].
gate5.decider_reason: The business fails the scale and valuation screens required for a direct Buffett investment and resides in an area of high structural uncertainty.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The requirement for escalating, perpetual reinvestment in a competitive digital landscape makes it difficult to ascertain a durable moat or stable intrinsic value.

valuation.owner_earnings: not in pack; approx $0.83/share based on Q2 2025 [D02, D04]
valuation.downside_case: Permanent loss of competitive advantage due to rising subscriber acquisition costs and AI-driven distribution threats [D05, D06]

drivers.driver: The company trades at a 24-28x earnings multiple [D04], offering an initial yield of 3.48% [D03] that is inadequate relative to the risks and the risk-free return available on our cash [D08].
The business model demands escalating, perpetual reinvestment in journalism and customer acquisition to sustain its subscriber base, which undermines the quality of its economics [D01, D05].
Competitive threats from free digital alternatives and generative AI create significant uncertainty regarding the long-term durability of the company's pricing power and moat [D06].
The dual-class governance structure limits outside shareholder influence, complicating our ability to assess alignment between management and the owners we represent [D01, D05].

kill_criteria: Permanent loss of pricing power due to AI-driven, free information alternatives [D06]
Subscriber acquisition costs increasing faster than ARPU growth, indicating an eroding moat [D05]
Management allocates capital toward non-journalistic growth initiatives outside the core competency [D01]
Structural decline in digital engagement leads to higher churn rates than currently modeled [D05]
final.what_would_change_our_mind: We would need to see evidence that the company's journalism and marketing reinvestment requirements stabilize as a percentage of revenue, and that the digital subscriber base proves resilient to free, AI-generated alternatives at a valuation providing a clear margin of safety [D05, D06].
final.memo:
We have reviewed The New York Times Company, a business focused on a journalism-based bundle including games, cooking, and news [D01]. While the company has shown a steady revenue trend of $2.59 billion in 2024 [D01, D02], the underlying economics remain challenging due to the constant need to reinvest in journalism and customer acquisition [D01, D05]. 

A durable competitive advantage in this digital landscape is difficult to identify because the product competes against an ocean of free, AI-distributed information [D06]. Rising subscriber acquisition costs indicate that maintaining growth requires ever-increasing capital, a characteristic we typically avoid [D01, D05]. 

Management has navigated the transition from print to digital effectively thus far, yet the dual-class governance structure leaves us with questions regarding the alignment of management with all owners [D01, D05]. We prefer to invest in businesses where we can clearly discern the long-term earnings power and the capital required to sustain it [D01]. 

At a valuation of roughly 25-29 times earnings, the price currently offered by Mr. Market does not provide the margin of safety we demand [D04]. With Berkshire holding significant liquidity in risk-free Treasuries, we find no reason to commit capital to a business facing such high structural uncertainty [D08]. We will continue to watch from the sidelines.
